title: Electrical power and energy — how your devices transfer energy
examTip: Multi-step calculation questions are common. Write down what you know and pick the right equation. Substitute carefully, and always include units. Practice is the only way to get fast at this.
introTips: Before you start: can you write down P = IV, E = Pt and V = IR from memory? If not, that is your first job.
Before reading, try estimating the power of five appliances at home. Then check how close you were.
Watch the unit conversions: watts ↔ kilowatts, minutes ↔ seconds. These trip people up in exams.
intro: Every time you boil a kettle, stream a video or charge your phone, energy is transferred by electrical work. Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers. Power tells you how fast an appliance transfers energy. It shows why a high-power kettle boils water faster. These equations also come up in almost every electricity exam question.

basics.text: Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It makes things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy, but you can see what it does.
A rate tells you how much happens each second. Speed is a rate: how many metres you travel each second.
Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second. Think of cars passing under a bridge: more cars each second is a bigger flow. It is measured in amperes (A), often called amps.
Potential difference is the push that makes charge move round a circuit. A cell or battery gives it. It is measured in volts (V), and a bigger number means a bigger push.

Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something. It is like a narrow, crowded corridor that slows people down. More resistance means less current for the same push. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself. 3 squared, written 3², is 3 × 3 = 9.
Energy can be kept in different ways, called energy stores. A moving thing has energy in its kinetic store. A hot thing has energy in its thermal store.
Physics equations use time in seconds. There are 60 seconds in a minute and 3600 seconds in an hour.

keyPoints.heading: Electrical power
keyPoints.content: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. It is how many joules are transferred per second. The unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. The key equations are: - P = IV (power = potential difference × current) - P = I²R (put V = IR into P = IV) Worked example 1: a kettle with I = 10 A and V = 230 V → P = 10 × 230 = 2300 W = 2.3 kW. Worked example 2: a phone charger with I = 1 A, V = 5 V → P = 1 × 5 = 5 W. Worked example 3: a resistor with R = 20 Ω and I = 3 A → P = 3² × 20 = 9 × 20 = 180 W. 1 kW = 1000 W. The power rating tells you how much energy an appliance transfers each second. A higher power kettle transfers more energy to the water each second. So the water's thermal energy store fills faster. In the same way, a higher power electric motor transfers more energy to its kinetic energy store each second.
writeBullets: Power — the rate of energy transfer. Measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 J/s
P = IV (the main equation: power = potential difference × current)
P = I²R (substitute V = IR into P = IV)
Higher power rating → more energy transferred each second
Kettle: I = 10 A, V = 230 V → P = 2300 W = 2.3 kW

keyTerms.def: The rate of energy transfer; measured in watts (W). P = IV.
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
1000 watts; used for higher-power appliances like kettles and heaters.

keyPoints.memTip: PIV: Power = I × V. Think of it as 'PIV-ot', the central equation everything else turns around.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often use P = IV and forget P = I²R. Use P = I²R when the potential difference is not given. Both are the same equation in different forms. There is no new physics, just algebra.

keyPoints.heading: Electrical energy
keyPoints.content: Energy transferred = power × time: E = Pt. The units are joules (J) when P is in watts (W) and t is in seconds (s). Putting in P = IV gives E = IVt. Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers. They transfer energy from batteries or the ac mains. In an electric motor, the energy goes to a kinetic energy store. In a heating device, it goes to a thermal energy store. The energy transferred depends on the power of the appliance and how long it is on. Worked example 1: a 2 kW kettle running for 3 minutes → E = 2000 × (3 × 60) = 2000 × 180 = 360,000 J = 360 kJ. Worked example 2: a 60 W bulb left on for 1 hour → E = 60 × 3600 = 216,000 J = 216 kJ.
writeBullets: E = Pt (energy = power × time). Joules when P is in W and t in seconds
Always convert time to seconds before using joules
Appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains — to a kinetic store (motor) or a thermal store (heater)

keyTerms.def: The total energy moved from one store to another; E = Pt, in joules.
The SI unit of energy; 1 J = 1 W × 1 s.

keyPoints.memTip: Joules = watts × seconds. Always convert time to seconds first.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Always convert time to seconds before working out energy in joules. Forgetting this is the most common mistake in energy calculations.

keyPoints.heading: Linking all the electrical equations
keyPoints.content: Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. In a multi-step calculation, you need to choose and combine equations. Here is how they all link together: - V = IR (potential difference = current × resistance) - P = IV (power). Substituting gives P = I²R - E = Pt (energy = power × time). Substituting gives E = IVt - Q = It (charge flow = current × time; Q in coulombs, C) - E = QV (energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference). This is the energy transferred by electrical work Worked example: a charge flow of 4 C moves through a potential difference of 6 V. E = QV = 4 × 6 = 24 J. Multi-step strategy: (1) write down all the values you know (2) find what the question asks for (3) choose the equation that links what you know to what you need (4) substitute values (5) rearrange if needed (6) check units Worked multi-step example: a resistor has R = 50 Ω and V = 10 V. Find the energy transferred in 2 minutes. Step 1: I = V/R = 10/50 = 0.2 A. Step 2: P = IV = 0.2 × 10 = 2 W. Step 3: E = Pt = 2 × 120 = 240 J.
writeBullets: V = IR — links potential difference, current and resistance
P = IV — power. Leads to P = I²R by substitution
E = Pt = IVt — energy transferred, in joules
Q = It — charge flow (coulombs) = current × time
E = QV — energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference. Links work done to circuit quantities
Multi-step strategy: list knowns → pick equation → substitute → rearrange → check units

keyTerms.def: The charge that flows past a point; Q = It. Unit: coulombs (C).
Energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V). Connects the electrical quantities to the concept of work done.
A calculation requiring two or more equations applied in sequence.

keyPoints.memTip: Draw a spider diagram with P in the middle. Draw the equations coming out from it: P=IV, P=I²R, E=Pt. Then link V=IR as the bridge between them.
keyPoints.tutor_note: E = QV is a core equation. You must be able to recall it and apply it. It is just energy = work done to move charge Q through a potential difference V.

0.question: A hairdryer has a resistance of 23 Ω and draws a current of 10 A. What is its power?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! P = I²R = 10² × 23 = 100 × 23 = 2300 W = 2.3 kW. This is the right equation when you have current and resistance but not potential difference.
0.wrongFeedback: Use P = I²R. Square the current first (10² = 100), then multiply by resistance (100 × 23 = 2300 W). P = IV would also work. First find V = IR = 10 × 23 = 230 V, then P = 10 × 230 = 2300 W.

1.question: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 60 s. How much energy does it transfer?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. E = Pt = 2000 × 60 = 120,000 J. Power in watts and time in seconds give energy in joules.
1.wrongFeedback: Use E = Pt (energy = power × time). E = 2000 W × 60 s = 120,000 J. Multiply, don't divide or add.

2.question: A current of 2 A flows for 10 s through a potential difference of 6 V. How much energy is transferred?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Step 1: Q = It = 2 × 10 = 20 C. Step 2: E = QV = 20 × 6 = 120 J.
2.wrongFeedback: This needs two equations. Step 1: charge flow Q = It = 2 × 10 = 20 C. Step 2: E = QV = 20 × 6 = 120 J.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert time to seconds when working out energy in joules (E = Pt). Three minutes is 180 s, not 3 s.
Using P = I + V, or some made-up equation, instead of P = IV. Power is a product (multiplication), not a sum.
Forgetting to square the current in P = I²R. Writing P = IR instead of P = I²R gives the potential difference, not the power.
Leaving units out of answers. Mark schemes need the correct unit (W, J) as well as the number.
examTips: In multi-step electricity calculations, always write out every step. Examiners give marks for correct working, even if your final answer is wrong. Never skip steps.
When a question gives you R and I, use P = I²R straight away. Don't work out V first and then use P = IV. It is faster and gives fewer chances for arithmetic slips.
